Warm-Up Questions

Reading

Part 1: Why Water Alone Is Not Enough

Water is very good at cleaning many things.

But water and oil do not mix.

When you pour oil into water, the oil floats on top.

It does not go into the water.

This means if you rub greasy hands with only water, the grease stays on your skin.

The water just moves around it.

According to the CDC, washing with only water is less effective than washing with soap.

Reading

Part 2: Soap Has Two Special Ends

A soap molecule is very small — too small to see.

But it has two ends that do different jobs.

One end loves water.

The other end loves oil and fat.

Because of this, soap can connect to both water and oil at the same time.

Think of soap as a tiny bridge between two things that do not usually mix.

The American Chemical Society explains that this is why soap works where water alone cannot.

Reading

Part 3: How Soap Traps the Grease

When you lather soap on your hands, many soap molecules move toward the grease.

Their oil-loving ends grab onto the grease.

At the same time, their water-loving ends point outward toward the water.

The soap molecules form a tiny round group called a micelle.

The grease is trapped inside the micelle.

According to the American Chemical Society, these micelles let water carry the trapped grease away when you rinse.

Reading

Part 4: Why Lathering and Rubbing Matter

Rubbing your hands together with soap is very important.

Rubbing helps the soap molecules reach all parts of your hands — between your fingers and under your nails.

Lathering also helps lift germs and chemicals off the skin.

The CDC says that lather and rubbing help remove germs and chemicals, and that very hot water is not needed.

Cool or warm water works well.
